title: A finite product of normal rings is normal
statement: Let $R_1,\dots,R_n$ be commutative normal rings [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Then their finite product $R=\prod_iR_i$ is a normal ring: for every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$, the localization $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is a normal domain.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0CYA (lemma-finite-product-normal, line 8260), with its proof

proof.text: Let $I$ be the finite index set of factors and let $\mathfrak p$ be any prime ideal of $R=\prod_{i\in I}R_i$. By [lem-weil-pbc-product-prime-factor] there are an index $i\in I$ and a prime ideal $\mathfrak q\subset R_i$ for which $\mathfrak p=\pi_i^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. This also deals with $I=\varnothing$: the asserted existence of $i$ contradicts emptiness, so the zero product ring has no primes and the normal-ring condition is vacuous.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0CYA (lemma-finite-product-normal), proof, lines 8263-8269; product-spectrum classification is Lemma Tag 00ED (lemma-spec-product), lines 3822-3848

proof.text: For the index and prime just obtained, [lem-weil-pbc-product-prime-localization] identifies $R_{\mathfrak p}$ with $(R_i)_{\mathfrak q}$ through the map induced by the coordinate projection. The hypothesis that $R_i$ is a normal ring means precisely, by [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], that $(R_i)_{\mathfrak q}$ is a normal domain.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0CYA (lemma-finite-product-normal), proof, lines 8269-8272; normal-ring definition Tag 00GV

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-normal-domain-ring-equivalence] to the isomorphism of step 2. It makes $R_{\mathfrak p}$ a normal domain. Since $\mathfrak p$ was arbitrary, the defining condition [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] holds for $R$.
